p.src: The bell rang, and the lecturer left the classroom. Sanshirō shook his ink-stained pen and was about to close his notebook. Then Yojirō, who was sitting beside him, spoke up. “Hey, lend me that a moment. I missed something.” Yojirō pulled Sanshirō’s notebook toward him and peered down at it. The words “stray sheep” were scribbled all over it. “What’s this?” “I got tired of taking notes on the lecture, so I was doodling.” “You shouldn’t be so careless about your studies. He said something about Kant’s transcendental idealism and Berkeley’s transcendental realism, didn’t he?” “Something like that.” “Weren’t you listening?” “No.” “You really are a stray sheep. There’s no helping you.” Yojirō gathered up his own notebook and rose. As he moved away from the desk, he said to Sanshirō, “Hey, come with me a moment.” Sanshirō followed Yojirō out of the classroom. They went down the stairs and came to the lawn before the entrance. A great cherry tree stood there. The two sat beneath it. At the beginning of summer, clover covered this whole place. When Yojirō had come to the office with his application for admission, two students were lying beneath this cherry tree. One told the other, “If they’d let me take the oral examination in dodoitsu verse, I could sing them any number of answers,” whereupon the other sang softly, “Before a learned doctor of elegant judgment, I should like to sit an examination in love.” Ever since then, Yojirō had been fond of the spot beneath this cherry tree, and whenever something came up, he dragged Sanshirō out here. When Yojirō told him this history, Sanshirō thought it only natural that Yojirō should translate “pity’s love” with a popular ditty. Today, however, Yojirō was unusually serious.

p.src: “What do you think?” he said. Sanshirō looked and saw the title “The Great Darkness” printed in large type. Below it was the pen name Mukago. “The Great Darkness” was the phrase Yojirō always used to describe Professor Hirota, and Sanshirō had heard it from him two or three times. But Mukago was a name wholly unknown to him. When asked what he thought, Sanshirō first looked at Yojirō’s face before attempting an answer. Without saying a word, Yojirō thrust his flat face forward, pressed the tip of his right forefinger to the end of his nose, and held still. A student standing some distance away saw this and began to grin. Noticing him, Yojirō finally took his finger from his nose. “I wrote it,” he said. Then Sanshirō understood. “Is this what you were writing when we went to see the chrysanthemum figures?” “No, that was only two or three days ago. It couldn’t possibly have been set in type so quickly. That one will appear next month. I wrote this one long ago. You can tell what it’s about from the title, can’t you?” “Professor Hirota?” “Yes. First I’ll stir up public opinion this way. Then I’ll prepare the ground for the professor to enter the university…” “Is that magazine so influential?” Sanshirō had never even heard its name. “No, the trouble is that it has no influence at all,” Yojirō replied. Sanshirō could not help smiling. “About how many copies does it sell?” Yojirō would not say how many. “Well, never mind. Writing something is better than writing nothing,” he said in his own defense. As Sanshirō gradually drew out the story, he learned that Yojirō had long been involved with the magazine and contributed to nearly every issue whenever he had time; but because he changed his pen name with every issue, no one knew it except two or three fellow contributors. That was understandable enough.

p.src: When Sanshirō bluntly asked whether he was doing the work partly to earn a little spending money, Yojirō's eyes widened. “You have only just come out of the Kyushu countryside, so you say such carefree things because you know nothing of the trends in the central literary world. Standing at the heart of the present world of ideas and witnessing its violent upheavals, how could anyone with a mind of his own pretend not to notice? In fact, literary authority today rests entirely in the hands of us young men, so wouldn't it be a waste not to step forward and say every word and half-word we can? The literary world is undergoing a dazzling revolution with headlong speed. Everything is in motion, every last thing, advancing toward a new current; it would be disastrous to be left behind. Unless we take the initiative and create this new current ourselves, there is no point in being alive. People toss around the word literature as though it were something cheap, but that is the sort of literature you hear about at universities. What we call the new literature is the great reflection of life itself. The new current in literature must influence the activity of Japanese society as a whole. Indeed, it is already doing so. While they nap and dream, it is steadily influencing them without their knowing it. It is a formidable thing. …” Sanshirō listened in silence. It struck him as something of a boast. Yet boast or not, Yojirō was delivering it with remarkable fervor. At least Yojirō himself appeared perfectly serious. Sanshirō was considerably moved. “So that is the spirit in which you do it? Then I suppose you do not care at all about being paid for your articles.” “Oh, I collect my fees. I take as much as I can get. But the magazine does not sell, so they are very reluctant to pay. We have to find some way of making it sell a little better. Can you think of any good scheme?” This time he turned to Sanshirō for advice. The conversation had abruptly descended to practical matters.

p.src: “At any rate, I will give you a copy of this magazine, so read it. The title ‘The Great Darkness’ is interesting, isn't it? A title like that is bound to startle people. —If you do not startle them, they will not read it, and that is no good.” The two men went in through the entrance, entered the classroom, and took their seats at their desks. Before long, the professor arrived. They both began taking notes. Unable to put “The Great Darkness” out of his mind, Sanshirō left the literary review open beside his notebook and began reading it between bouts of note-taking, taking care that the professor did not notice. Fortunately, the professor was nearsighted. Moreover, he was completely absorbed in his own lecture. He paid no attention whatsoever to Sanshirō's misconduct. Emboldened, Sanshirō alternated between taking notes here and reading there; but doing alone what properly required two people was an impossible feat, and in the end he lost the thread of both “The Great Darkness” and the lecture notes. Only one sentence from Yojirō's article lodged clearly in his mind. “How many long years did nature spend creating a jewel? And for how many long years did that jewel shine in silence before fortune allowed it to be mined?” That was the sentence. The rest remained incomprehensible. On the other hand, he got through the entire class without writing the words stray sheep even once. The instant the lecture ended, Yojirō turned to Sanshirō and asked, “Well?” When Sanshirō replied that in truth he had not yet read it properly, Yojirō reproached him as a man who knew nothing of economizing time. He insisted that Sanshirō must read it. Sanshirō promised that he would be sure to read it when he got home. Before long, it was noon. The two left the gate together. “You will be there tonight, won't you?” Yojirō stopped at the corner of the side street leading into Nishikatamachi. That evening there was to be a gathering of their classmates. Sanshirō had forgotten about it.

p.src: When he returned to his lodgings, took a bath, and emerged feeling pleasantly refreshed, he found a picture postcard on his desk. It depicted a stream bordered by thick, tangled grass, with two sheep lying on the bank and, beyond them, a large man standing with a walking stick. The man's face was exceedingly ferocious. He was plainly modeled on the devils in Western pictures, and, to remove all doubt, the word “devil” was neatly written in kana beside him. On the front, beneath Sanshirō's name and address, only the words “lost child” had been written in small letters. Sanshirō understood at once who the lost child was. More than that, he was delighted that she had drawn two lost sheep on the back of the card, tacitly casting him as one of them. Mineko was not the only lost child; he himself had naturally been included as well. That, it seemed, had been Mineko's intention. Only now did the meaning of Mineko's phrase “stray sheep” become clear to him. He meant to read “The Great Darkness,” as he had promised Yojirō, but for the moment he could not bring himself to begin. He kept gazing at the postcard and pondering it. It had a comic spirit unlike anything even in Aesop. It also seemed innocent. It was witty, too. And beneath it all lay something that stirred Sanshirō's heart. Even in its execution, it was thoroughly admirable. Everything had been made perfectly clear. Yoshiko's drawing of the persimmon tree could not compare with it. —So it seemed to Sanshirō. After a while, Sanshirō finally began reading “The Great Darkness.” In truth, he began in a distracted frame of mind, but after two or three pages he was gradually drawn in; before he knew it, he had passed five pages, then six, and at last finished the twenty-seven-page essay without the least difficulty.

p.src: But the next moment, when he asked himself what he had read, there was nothing. There was so completely nothing that it was almost comical. He merely felt that he had read a great deal, and read it with tremendous vigor. Sanshirō was impressed by Yojirō's skill. The essay began by attacking contemporary men of letters and ended by praising Professor Hirota. It was especially scathing in its abuse of the Westerner in the literature department. Unless a suitable Japanese scholar were promptly invited to give lectures worthy of a university, the university—the highest seat of learning—would soon become no better than an old-fashioned temple school, scarcely distinguishable from a mummy of brick and stone. Of course, nothing could be done if no such person existed—but here was Professor Hirota. For ten unchanging years, he had taught at the Higher School, content to endure poor pay and obscurity. Yet he was a true scholar. He was the very man to assume a professorship, contribute fresh vitality to the world of learning, and bring scholarship into contact with Japan's living society. —Reduced to its essence, that was all it said; yet this scant content had been stretched across twenty-seven pages by an exceedingly plausible tone and a profusion of glittering epigrams. It contained a great many amusing lines: “Only old men boast of baldness”; “Venus was born from the waves, but men of true discernment are not born from universities”; and “To regard doctors as the learned world's celebrated product is like regarding jellyfish as the celebrated product of Tago Bay.” But apart from those, there was nothing at all. What was particularly odd was that, after likening Professor Hirota to the Great Darkness, Yojirō compared the other scholars to round paper lanterns that could do no more than dimly illuminate a space of two feet square at most—writing exactly what Hirota himself had once said to him. And he had gone out of his way to add, just as before, that round paper lanterns and pipe bowls were all relics of a bygone age and entirely useless to young men like themselves.

p.src: On reflection, Yojirō's essay had a certain vitality. He wrote as though he alone represented the new Japan, and while reading it, one could not help being carried along. Yet it had no substance at all. It was like a war waged without a base of operations. Moreover, viewed unfavorably, the way it was written might even suggest an ulterior strategy. Country-bred Sanshirō could not immediately discern that particular flaw, but after reading it and searching his own feelings, he sensed a lingering dissatisfaction somewhere within him. He picked up Mineko's picture postcard again and began gazing at the two sheep and that same devil. Here, by contrast, everything gave him pleasure. This pleasure made his earlier dissatisfaction stand out all the more sharply. So he gave no further thought to the essay. He thought he would send Mineko a reply. Unfortunately, he could not draw. He decided to put his reply into words. If he used words, however, they would have to be worthy of this picture postcard. Such words did not readily come to mind. While he dawdled over it, four o'clock came and went.

p.src: “You say it is contrivance, but all I do is arrange things beforehand through human effort so that nature can follow its proper course. That is entirely different from plotting some senseless scheme that defies nature. I do not care if you call it contrivance. Contrivance itself is not wrong. It is bad contrivance that is wrong.” Sanshirō could not utter a word in reply. He felt as though he had some objection, but could not put it into words. Only the part of Yojirō’s argument that he himself had not yet considered stood out clearly in his mind. Sanshirō was, if anything, impressed by that. “I suppose that is true,” he replied with considerable vagueness, and they set off again, walking shoulder to shoulder. Once they entered the main gate, the view suddenly opened wide before them. Large buildings stood here and there, black against the night. Where the sharply defined roofs ended, the clear sky began. The stars were innumerable. “What a beautiful sky,” said Sanshirō. Yojirō too walked on for about six feet, looking up at the sky. Suddenly he called to Sanshirō, “Hey, you.” Thinking he was about to resume their earlier conversation, Sanshirō answered, “What is it?” “What do you feel when you look at a sky like this?” It was an oddly uncharacteristic thing for Yojirō to say. He had any number of ready-made answers about infinity and eternity, but Sanshirō kept silent, thinking Yojirō would laugh if he said anything of the sort. “How petty we are. Perhaps I should stop carrying on this campaign after tomorrow. Writing ‘The Great Darkness’ does not seem likely to do any good.” “Why have you suddenly started talking like that?” “This sky puts such thoughts into my head. —Have you ever been in love with a woman?” Sanshirō could not answer at once. “Women are frightening creatures,” said Yojirō. “They are frightening. I know that too,” said Sanshirō. At that, Yojirō burst into loud laughter.

Today in particular was warm. Sanshirō went to the bathhouse in the morning. In a world where few people have time to spare, the bathhouse was remarkably empty in the morning. Sanshirō looked at an advertisement for the Mitsukoshi dry-goods store hanging in the wooden-floored room. It depicted a beautiful woman. Her face looked somewhat like Mineko’s. On closer inspection, however, the expression in her eyes was different. There was no telling what her teeth were like. What had struck Sanshirō most about Mineko’s face was the look in her eyes and the alignment of her teeth. According to Yojirō, her teeth protruded a little, which was why they were always showing like that, but Sanshirō could not believe it at all. … Sanshirō had been thinking about all this while soaking in the bath, and left without washing himself very thoroughly. Since the previous evening, his awareness of himself as a young man of the new age had suddenly grown intense; but only the awareness was intense—his body remained just as it had been. Whenever there was a holiday, he took things much easier than the others. That afternoon he intended to go and watch the university athletics meet. Sanshirō had never been particularly fond of sports. Back home, he had gone rabbit hunting two or three times. He had also once served as a flag signaler at a high-school rowing regatta. On that occasion he had confused the blue flag with the red one, provoking a great many complaints. To be fair, the professor responsible for firing the finishing pistol had failed to fire it properly. He did fire it, but it made no sound. That was what had caused Sanshirō to panic.

p.src: He set out after noon. The entrance to the grounds was at the southern corner of the athletic field. A large Japanese flag and a British flag were crossed above it. The Japanese flag made sense, but he could not understand what the British flag was for. Sanshirō wondered whether it might be because of the Anglo-Japanese Alliance. But he had not the slightest idea what connection there could be between the Anglo-Japanese Alliance and a university track-and-field meet. The athletic field was a rectangular stretch of lawn. As autumn was already far advanced, the grass had faded considerably. The spectators' area was on the west side. With a large artificial hill rising across the whole rear and the fence of the field closing off the front, it was arranged so that everyone was herded into the space between. There were far too many spectators for such a narrow space, and it was exceedingly cramped. Fortunately, the weather was fine, so it was not cold. Even so, quite a few people were wearing overcoats. On the other hand, some women had come carrying parasols. What disappointed Sanshirō was that the women's section was separate and inaccessible to ordinary people. He was also disappointed to find so many imposing men in frock coats and the like gathered there, making his own influence seem unexpectedly slight. Sanshirō, who considered himself a young man of the new age, felt rather diminished. Even so, he did not forget to peer between the people toward the women's section. It was hard to see well from the side, but that section was indeed a pretty sight. Every one of the women was dressed in her finest. Moreover, at that distance all their faces looked beautiful. But by the same token, no one woman stood out as especially beautiful. Only the whole was beautiful as a whole. It was the beauty by which women conquer men. It was not the beauty by which one woman triumphs over another. At this, Sanshirō was disappointed again. Still, thinking that if he looked carefully they must be somewhere, he surveyed the section closely and, sure enough, found the two of them sitting side by side in the front row, at the spot nearest the fence.

p.src: Now that Sanshirō finally knew where to direct his gaze, he relaxed as though one matter had been settled, when suddenly five or six men burst into view before him. The two-hundred-metre race had just ended. The finish line was directly in front of Mineko and Yoshiko and almost under their noses, so these strapping fellows inevitably entered Sanshirō's field of vision as he stared at the two women. The five or six soon increased to twelve or thirteen. They all appeared to be breathing hard. Sanshirō compared the bearing of these students with his own and was astonished by the difference. He wondered how they could ever bring themselves to run with such reckless abandon. Yet all the ladies were watching intently. Mineko and Yoshiko seemed the most intent of all. Sanshirō began to feel that he, too, would like to try running with such reckless abandon. The first-place runner, wearing purple running shorts, stood facing the women's section. Looking closely, Sanshirō saw that he resembled the student who had made a speech at the social gathering the previous evening. With height like that, no wonder he had come first. The timekeeper wrote “25.74 seconds” on the blackboard. When he had finished writing, he tossed away the remaining chalk and turned this way; Sanshirō saw that it was Nonomiya. Nonomiya was wearing an unusually jet-black frock coat, with an official's badge pinned to his chest, and looked quite distinguished. He took out a handkerchief and brushed the sleeve of his coat two or three times, then presently left the blackboard and came across the lawn. He came out directly in front of where Mineko and Yoshiko were sitting. From the far side of the low fence, he craned his neck into the women's section and said something. Mineko stood up. She walked over to Nonomiya. They appeared to begin talking from opposite sides of the fence. Mineko suddenly turned around. Her face was filled with a delighted smile.

p.src: Surely no event requires as much strength as the shot put. And for all the strength it requires, few things could be less interesting. They simply throw a shot, just as the name says. There is no skill or artistry to it at all. Standing by the railing, Nonomiya watched for a moment and laughed. But he must have thought he might obstruct the spectators’ view. He left the railing and withdrew onto the field. The two women also returned to their former seats. Every so often, another shot was thrown. To begin with, Sanshirō could scarcely tell how far any of them went. Sanshirō began to find it absurd. Even so, he endured it and remained standing there. At long last it seemed to be over, and Nonomiya once again wrote 11.38 metres on the blackboard. Then came another race, followed by the long jump, and after that the hammer throw began. By the time they reached the hammer throw, Sanshirō could bear it no longer. Athletic meets were things people ought to hold privately, each on their own. They were not meant to be shown to others. He even convinced himself that every woman who watched such things with enthusiasm was thoroughly misguided, then slipped out of the grounds and made his way to the artificial hill at the rear. A curtain had been hung there, blocking the way. He turned back and walked a little way along the gravel, where a few others who had escaped from the grounds were strolling here and there. There were elegantly dressed ladies among them. Sanshirō turned right again and climbed the rising path to the top of the hill. The path ended at the summit. There was a large rock there. Sanshirō sat down on it and gazed at the pond below the high cliff. From the athletic field below came a great roar from the crowd. Sanshirō sat absentmindedly on the rock for about five minutes. Presently he felt like moving again and rose; as he stood adjusting the heels of his shoes, he caught sight of the women from before among the lightly tinted maple leaves at the foot of the slope. They were walking side by side along the foot of the hill.

p.src: From above, Sanshirō looked down at the two women. They emerged through a gap in the branches into the clear sunlight. If he said nothing, they would pass right by him. Sanshirō wondered whether he should call out to them. The distance was much too great. He hurried two or three steps down the grass toward the foot of the hill. Just as he began descending, one of the women conveniently turned toward him. At that, Sanshirō stopped. The truth was, he had little desire to court their favor by greeting them first. The athletic meet had irritated him somewhat. “Up there of all places...” Yoshiko called out. She was smiling in surprise. Sanshirō felt that this woman looked at even the most commonplace thing as though it were a novelty. Conversely, he imagined that however extraordinary a thing she encountered, she would greet it with the same look, as though she had been expecting it all along. That was why being with her never felt in the least oppressive, yet still gave him a sense of calm. Standing there, Sanshirō decided that it was entirely due to those large, perpetually moist, dark eyes. Mineko stopped as well. She looked at Sanshirō. But on this occasion her eyes alone conveyed nothing at all. It was as though she were gazing at a tall tree. Sanshirō felt inwardly as though he were looking at a lamp whose flame had gone out. He stood rooted to the same spot. Mineko did not move either. “Why aren’t you watching the events?” Yoshiko called up from below. “I was watching until just now, but it was so dull that I left.” Yoshiko looked back at Mineko. Mineko’s expression remained unchanged. Sanshirō said, “More to the point, why did the two of you come out? Weren’t you watching with tremendous enthusiasm?” He spoke loudly, though it was hard to tell whether the barb had hit its mark. Only then did Mineko smile a little. Sanshirō could not quite understand what her smile meant.

p.src: Sanshirō was more surprised than anything by Nonomiya’s easygoing attitude. If it was so easy for him to return to life in lodgings, surely he would have been better off never setting up a household in the first place. He even found himself wondering about such irrelevant matters as what they had done with their pots, kettles, buckets, and other household goods. But it was hardly worth saying aloud, so he offered no particular comment. Moreover, Nonomiya’s retreat from being the head of a household to a mode of life resembling that of an ordinary student meant, in effect, that he had moved one step farther away from the family system. For Sanshirō, this was a welcome development, as though an immediate nuisance had been shifted somewhat farther into the distance. On the other hand, Yoshiko had moved in with Mineko. This brother and sister seemed made in such a way that they could not be content unless they were constantly going back and forth between one another. And while they kept going back and forth, the relationship between Nonomiya and Mineko would gradually change. Then there was no telling when the time might come for Nonomiya to give up lodging-house life for good. While speaking with Mineko, Sanshirō pictured this uncertain future in his mind. He had no heart for the conversation at all. Trying to make even his outward manner appear normal became painful. Just then, as luck would have it, Yoshiko returned. The two women discussed going back to watch the events once more, but the shortening autumn day was already far advanced, and as it waned the chill of the broad open air steadily deepened, so they decided to go home. Sanshirō, too, meant to part from the women and return to his lodgings, but the three of them drifted off together as they talked, leaving him no opportunity for a definite farewell. The two women seemed to be drawing him along with them.

p.src: “People like Sōhachi are beyond the understanding of ordinary people like us. He lives on a far higher plane, contemplating great matters,” she said, launching into lavish praise of Nonomiya. Yoshiko listened in silence. Scholars avoid tiresome worldly obligations and endure as simple a life as possible because their research leaves them no choice, so it cannot be helped. That a man like Nonomiya, whose work was renowned even abroad, should live in the same sort of lodgings as an ordinary student only proved how great he was; the dirtier his lodgings, the more he deserved to be revered. Such, in broad outline, was the rest of Mineko’s eulogy of Nonomiya. Sanshirō parted from the two women at the Red Gate. As he turned toward Oiwake, he began to think. Mineko was indeed quite right. When he compared himself with Nonomiya, there was a vast difference between them. He had only just come up from the country and entered the university. He possessed neither learning worthy of the name nor any real discernment. It was only natural that Mineko could not accord him the same respect she showed Nonomiya. Come to think of it, he even felt that she might be making a fool of him. Earlier, when he had answered on the hill that he was there because the athletic meet was dull, Mineko had looked serious and asked whether there was anything interesting up there. He had noticed nothing at the time, but viewed now, her words might have been a deliberate taunt. It dawned on Sanshirō that, when he reviewed one by one everything Mineko had said and done toward him up to that day, every last thing could be interpreted in a bad light. In the middle of the street, Sanshirō flushed crimson and lowered his head. When he suddenly looked up, he saw Yojirō approaching alongside the student who had given the speech at the gathering the previous night.
